prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The ground plane extends forward from the camera wearer, while the phone and hands are consistently the nearest surfaces, roughly 0.25–0.6 m away and within arm’s reach; the visible distant person near the top of frame 1 is several metres away, approximately 5–10 m. Brightness separates the foreground hands and phone from the receding pavement more clearly than RGB, but it does not reliably distinguish the phone from the hands because their depths are similar. Across the five frames, the phone stays in front of and below the wearer’s viewpoint, shifting from left toward the centre and then right, with no clear large approach or retreat. The hands partly occlude the phone in frames 2–4, and all foreground limbs are cut off by the bottom edge; depth near image borders and the distant background appears smooth and unreliable.
descriptions.segmentation: The map isolates the camera wearer’s hands/arms as person instances and the phone as a cell-phone instance, showing the phone above and partly behind the hands at roughly arm’s length, about 0.25–0.6 m from the camera. A separate person appears only at the upper edge of frame 1, far in front and slightly right of centre, but is mostly out of view, so facing direction and gaze toward the wearer cannot be determined. Across the strip, the phone moves from left-of-centre to centre and then right-of-centre while remaining close to the hands; the two hands are separated in frame 1, converge around the phone in frames 2–4, and only one foreground arm is clearly segmented in frame 5. The masks make object boundaries and hand–phone occlusion clearer than RGB, but they provide little metric distance, merge separate body parts into person regions, and the frame-1 “pizza” label plus the altered phone/person masks in frame 5 appear unreliable.
descriptions.pose: The skeleton map localizes the camera wearer’s hands: both hands are visible close together around the phone area in frames 2 and 4, mainly one hand is recovered in frames 3 and 5, and no reliable foreground skeleton appears in frame 1. The hand keypoints show fingers above the wrists and the hands oriented inward toward the phone, all within roughly 0.25–0.6 m of the camera and mutually within about 0.1–0.4 m; they do not establish whether any distant person faces or looks toward the wearer. In frame 4, a yellow body/arm skeleton lies to the left of the magenta hand skeletons and overlaps them, but because this is the wearer’s bottom-edge foreground limb region, its body assignment and exact orientation are uncertain. Pose makes joint arrangement and changing hand separation clearer than RGB, while missing joints, overlapping left/right hands, edge truncation, and inconsistent detections make frames 1, 3, and 5 especially unreliable.
